item.title: “I Never Really Thought of Insects as Beautiful Creatures” – Dara Ojo on Becoming a Macro Photographer
item.description: Nigerian Macro Photographer, Dara Ojo. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, Dara Ojo was stuck at home in China, like everyone else in the world. He had recently picked up photography, and that allowed him to explore and pay close attention to his immediate surroundings. One day, he started paying closer attention to the tiny creatures around him and was amazed by what he was seeing. There were colours, patterns, behaviours and details that he had never noticed before. It felt like discovering an entirely different world that had been right in front of me all along. Dara self-taught himself macro photography, and the seemingly small curiosity during the pandemic has grown into a journey of documenting biodiversity across Nigeria, Canada, Costa Rica, Mexico, Ecuador and beyond. His work has travelled globally and has been featured in major international publications. Dara has photographed over 40 types of spiders, 50 species of moths, 30 species of butterflies, more than 20 dragonflies, and at least 70 damselflies. There are many photographers in Nigeria, but seeing that macro photography is not often explored by Nigerians, we sat down for a brief conversation with Dara, where he shared what inspired his form of photography, what documenting biodiversity in different environments has taught him about nature and his forthcoming first photography book, Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem. Leafhopper infected by Metarhizium Fungus. Photo by Dara Ojo. Hey Dara, how are you feeling? I feel good. I feel blessed. Thank you for having me. What do you think inspired or attracted you to macro photography? Growing up in Nigeria, I never really thought of insects as something beautiful or worth photographing. Like many people, I saw them as creatures you either avoided or tried to get rid of. But once I started looking at them through my camera, my perspective completely changed. What fascinated me most wasn’t just how they looked, but how they lived. I started asking questions. Why does this spider behave this way? How does that tiny insect survive? What role does it play in nature? The more I discovered, the more curious I became. Six years later, that curiosity has taken me from photographing tiny creatures around my neighbourhood in China to exploring rainforests and other ecosystems across different continents. And the interesting thing is that I still experience that same excitement whenever I discover something new. I don’t think that feeling will ever go away. Bumblebee by macro photographer, Dara Ojo. The excitement. How can you describe it? When taking a shot, what do you feel that you hope people also feel when they encounter the photo? Wonder. That’s probably the best word to describe it. Sometimes I’m photographing a creature, and I genuinely cannot believe what I’m looking at. It might be the incredible colours of a jumping spider, the delicate patterns on a moth’s wings, or an insect doing something I’ve never witnessed before. T

item.description: To Adaego With Love leads Nigerian nominations for the 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards. Photo Credit: Nwamaka Chikezie/Instagram The nominations for the 22nd Africa Movie Academy Awards (AMAA) are out, and there’s already plenty to unpack ahead of the ceremony in Lagos this November. From Uganda and Kenya to Nigeria and South Africa, films from across the continent are competing for some of African cinema’s biggest honours. Leading this year’s nominations are Uganda’s Slum Bomber and Kenya’s One Woman , One Bra , with 14 nominations each. Nigeria is also well represented, with Nwamaka Chikezie ‘s To Adaego With Love earning 11 nominations, while Daniel Etim-Effiong ‘s The Herd follows closely with 10. They’re in good company. South Africa’s The Trek and Ben Made It , alongside Côte d’Ivoire’s Colours of Exile , have also received 10 nominations each, while Colours of Fire has nine. The nominees were announced during a livestream on AMAA’s official YouTube channel. Now, attention turns to the awards ceremony on 15 November 2026 at the Lagos Marriott Hotel, where filmmakers, actors and other industry professionals will gather to celebrate the year’s achievements in African cinema. item.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
item.description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

item.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
item.description: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...

When we first begin to talk, we learn to express our needs and understand the needs of others.
